name: Security remediation
description: Audit, fix and re-audit: Security finds and ranks the issues, Plan, Build and Verify fix them, and a final Security pass confirms each one is resolved without new regressions.

config.instructions: Audit the security of the scope in workflow_input.request. workflow_input.context, when it is not empty, holds results from earlier in this conversation (for example findings or a plan the user has reviewed or edited): treat it as established input and build on it instead of repeating it, but check anything that looks stale against the workspace. Identify the assets and trust boundaries, then inspect input handling, authentication and authorization, secrets and sensitive data, filesystem, network, command and database boundaries, dependencies and configuration. Rank each finding by likelihood and impact, with evidence (file and symbol), an attack scenario and a specific remediation; separate confirmed findings from theoretical risks, and never print secrets. Do not modify files or run commands. The next step receives only your final message, not your tool history, so keep every fact it needs.

Turn workflow_input.request and the supplied findings into an actionable implementation plan for a fresh Build session that receives only your final message, not your exploration history. Order the remediation by severity and tie each step to a finding in workflow_input.audit. Verify the key facts in the code first, and preserve the user's requirements, decisions and relevant findings. Return ordered, numbered steps, each naming the files and symbols to change, the exact change and an observable acceptance check, followed by risks and prerequisites, with optional work clearly labeled as optional. Do not implement anything or claim anything was tested. Ask the user only for decisions you cannot resolve from the request or the code. Do not modify files or run commands. The next step receives only your final message, not your tool history, so keep every fact it needs.

Implement the request following the supplied plan. Read the entire plan and use its ordered steps as a checklist. Use its findings for targeted file reads, then make the required changes. Do not replace implementation with another proposal. Read before editing, preserve existing work, follow project conventions and respect tool permissions. Adapt the plan only when the actual code requires it and explain why. Run relevant tests or other checks and fix recoverable failures. Finish with a written handoff describing what happened for each plan step, files changed, checks actually run and their results, deviations and remaining work. Clearly explain any blocker or unsuccessful attempt. Never imply unfinished or unverified work succeeded. The next agent receives this message, not your tool history. Use ordinary text or Markdown; no JSON format is required.

Review the original request, the plan and the Build handoff against the actual workspace. Inspect relevant code and run appropriate tests or checks with the available tools. Do not merely accept the Build claims. Do not edit files or run destructive commands. Check each required plan step and identify omissions, regressions and unverified claims. Finish with a clear written verdict: what was verified with evidence, what failed or remains blocked, and precise next actions. A blocked or incomplete build must be reported as such, not approved. Use ordinary text or Markdown; no JSON or status field is required.

Re-audit after the fix. workflow_input.audit holds the original findings, workflow_input.plan the remediation, and workflow_input.build and workflow_input.verify what was done and checked. For each original finding state whether it is resolved, partly resolved or still open, with evidence from the code; then look for new issues the changes introduced. End with a verdict and the residual risk. Do not modify files or run commands. Your final message is the workflow result the user will read and may act on, so make it complete and self-contained.
